messages.text: Sharma ji! Writing 1 Google Sept $525 Put at $22.40 gives me $2,240 instant cash for 100 shares! Isn't this how bank arbitrage desks print riskless money?
Careful, Raju! Writing a put obligates you to buy. If Google falls to $480, buying 100 shares at $525 causes a $4,500 gross loss—a $2,260 net loss after your $2,240 premium!

leftColumn.title: Futures & Forwards

bullets: Holder is committed (obligated) to buy or sell at maturity

bullets: Holder has the right, but zero obligation, to buy or sell

ui_state.question: A trader with $2,000 capital can either buy 100 shares of a $20 stock or buy 2,000 two-month call options with a $22.50 strike price at a $1.00 premium per option. If the stock rises to $27.00 at expiration, what is the trader's net option profit compared to the stock profit, and what happens if the stock falls to $15.00?
ui_state.answer: Spot on! At $27.00, each $22.50 call option is worth $4.50 at expiration, generating a $9,000 gross payoff across 2,000 options. Subtracting the $2,000 initial premium gives a net profit of $7,000—10 times higher than the $700 profit from holding 100 shares! However, if the stock drops to $15.00, the options expire worthless for a $2,000 loss (100% of capital) versus only a $500 loss on the shares.
